column2: The three other actions that remain are giving, study and sacrifice, which are joined with dharma.
The knower of dharma should be heedful in these three acts: self-controlled, friendly, patient, equal to all beings, a sage.
A pure brahmin who carries out all this as he is able, so joined, and a householder of strict vows, would win heaven.
The learned sage, devoted to his own dharma, with all senses restrained, intent on what is dear and good to his teacher, truthful, righteous and pure,
permitted by his teacher, should eat food without disparaging it, eating oblation-food and alms, with fixed station, seat and walks.
Offering to the fire at both twilights, pure and composed, he should always carry a bilva or palasha staff.
His garment should be linen, cotton, deer-skin, or all of ochre-red cloth.
He should wear a munja girdle, be matted-haired, bathe daily, wear the sacred thread, study, and keep his vows unbroken.
With purified waters he should always make offerings to the gods, restrained in feeling; such a celibate student is praised.
So disciplined, with seed held up, composed, he would win heaven; he does not revolve through births, having reached the highest place.
Refined by all rites and a celibate, leaving villages, the sage who has gone forth should live in the forest.
With roots, fruits and alms he should honour a guest who has come; from what he eats he should give alms, tireless, always.
He should always eat after gods and guests, silent, with unfaltering mind, eating lightly, depending on the gods.
Self-controlled, friendly, patient, keeping hair and beard, offering, devoted to study, truthful and righteous,
his body given up, always skilful, dwelling constantly in the forest, composed: so joined the forest-dweller, master of his senses, would win heaven.
A householder, a celibate student or a forest-dweller, whoever wishes to establish himself in liberation should take refuge in the highest way of life.
Having given freedom from fear to all beings, he should practise actionlessness, good to all beings, friendly, a sage with senses restrained.
What comes unasked, unplanned, by chance, he should always accept as food, a morsel that comes, free of longing.
He should eat just enough to keep going, solely for sustaining life, what is gained by dharma, and not follow desire.
Besides a morsel and a covering he should in no way take more; he should take only as much as he eats, and not otherwise.
He should not accept from others, nor ever give, the wise one, always sharing out of compassion for beings.
He should not take others' property, nor take what is not asked; having enjoyed any object, he should not long for it again.
Clay, water, stone, leaves, flowers and fruits, uncovered, available, he may take as needed.
He should not live by craft, nor desire two meals; he should not be a hater or a teacher, nor a performer; he should eat what is purified by faith, avoiding omens.
Free in livelihood, unattached, making no pact with any beings, with the fire out and people having eaten, he should go for alms.
When conduct is established and the dishes have fallen away, the knower of liberation should seek alms; he should not rejoice in gain, nor be dejected in loss.
Eating by measure, expecting the time, he should go for alms composed; he should not wish for a common gain, nor eat when honoured; the mendicant should shrink from gain that comes with honour.
He should not savour sour, acid, bitter, astringent, pungent or sweet flavours while eating; he should eat only to keep going, solely for sustaining life.
The knower of liberation should seek a living without obstructing beings, and should not beg after another while begging in any way.
He should not display dharma, should live in solitude free of passion, in an empty house, forest, tree-root, riverbank, or in a mountain cave for shelter.
He should stay one night in a village, in summer, or in the rainy season in one place; guided by the sun on the road, he should wander the earth like an insect.
Out of compassion for beings he should travel looking at the earth; he should not hoard, and should avoid dwelling in affection.
The knower of liberation should always do his tasks with purified water; he should always touch water that has been lifted up.
Non-harm, celibacy, truth, uprightness, freedom from anger and envy, self-control, and no slander always.
With his senses restrained, he should be devoted to these eight vows; he should always practise sinless, guileless, straight conduct.
He should neither do nor cause to be done acts joined with hope or with harm, nor works of collecting the world and dharma.
Passing beyond all states, light, he should wander, equal to all beings, immovable and moving.
He should not alarm anyone, nor be alarmed by anyone; trusted by all beings, he is called the foremost knower of liberation.
He should not brood on the future nor think of the past; he should disregard the present, awaiting time and composed.
He should never defile with eye, mind or word; he should do nothing wrong, seen or unseen.
Withdrawing the senses entirely, like a tortoise its limbs, with senses, mind and intellect exhausted, he should look on, free of senses.
Free of dualities, free of salutation, free of svaha and also svadha, free of possessiveness and ego, and free of acquisition and preservation,
without hope toward all beings, unattached, without support, all-knowing, freed everywhere, he is freed, without doubt.
Without hands, feet or back, without head or belly, with qualities and actions gone, alone, spotless, steady,
without smell, taste, touch, form or sound, without skin, bone, marrow or flesh,
free of anxiety, imperishable, eternal, always abiding in the heart; those who see the Self abiding in all beings are not dead.
Where the attainment of the knowing is held to be grasping without a mark, intellect does not go, nor senses, nor gods, nor Vedas, sacrifices, worlds, austerity or valour.
Therefore, markless, the knower of dharma, following the vow of dharma, hiding in dharma, the learned one should live a life unknown.
Not deluded, in the form of the deluded, he should practise dharma without harming it, so that others always despise him.
So behaving, he should practise dharma without defiling the path of the good; one endowed with such conduct is called the best sage.
The senses, the objects of the senses, the five great elements, mind, intellect, the Self, the unmanifest and the Person:
having fully reckoned all this and rightly abandoned it, stainless, he then reaches heaven, freed from all bonds.
At the last hour, the knower of truth, having reckoned this, should meditate in solitude and be freed, without support.
Freed from all attachments, like the wind moving in the sky, his treasury exhausted, fearless, he reaches the highest state.
Not far away is the supreme Brahman, resting on Vedic knowledge: free of dualities, free of qualities, eternal, inconceivable, the supreme secret.
By knowledge and austerity the steadfast see that state, their darkness washed away, purified, passion gone, spotless.
By austerity those who seek the highest travel the safe road, those knowers of Brahman always devoted to renunciation.
They say austerity is a lamp, conduct accomplishes dharma, but we hold knowledge to be supreme, and renunciation the best austerity.
One who knows unobstructed knowledge from certainty about reality, the Self abiding in all beings, is held to be a goal of all.
The learned one who sees dwelling together and dwelling apart, unity and plurality, is freed from sorrow.
One who desires nothing and despises nothing, living in this world, is fit to become Brahman.
Knowing the truth of Pradhana and the qualities, knowing the arrangement of all beings, without possessiveness and ego, he is freed, without doubt.
Free of dualities, free of salutation, free of svadha, he goes by calm alone to the eternal, free of qualities and dualities.
Having given up all action made of qualities, good and bad, having given up both truth and falsehood, the creature is freed, without doubt.
The great tree with the unmanifest seed as source, made of the trunk of intellect, with the branch of great ego, with hollows of the senses within,
with branches of the great elements and twigs of specifics, always leafed, flowered, with fruits of good and bad: this is the eternal Brahman-tree, the livelihood of all beings.
Having cut and split it with the supreme sword of knowledge, giving it up and gaining immortality, one would give up death and birth; without possessiveness and ego, he is freed, without doubt.
These two birds, eternal friends, are both insentient; one beyond these two is held the conscious one.

The insentient is joined with the aggregate of goodness; beyond goodness the inner Self is conscious: the knower of the field, whose understanding is the aggregate of goodness, passes beyond the qualities and is freed from the noose of death.
If even for the span of a breath at the end of life he is composed, approaching the Self, he becomes fit for immortality.
If even for a blink he restrains the Self in the Self, he attains by the Self's grace the imperishable gain of the wise.
Again and again restraining the vital breaths by breath-control, ten, twelve, even beyond twenty-four,
so, serene of soul, he first gains whatever he wishes; goodness surging from the unmanifest makes him fit for immortality.
The knowers here praise nothing higher than goodness. By inference we know the Person to rest in goodness; the Person cannot otherwise be reached, brahmins.
Patience, steadfastness, non-harm, equanimity, truth, uprightness, knowledge, renunciation: this is held as the conduct of goodness.
By this same inference the wise think goodness and the Person are one; there is no question about it.
Some learned ones, well established in knowledge, say that unity of the knower of the field and goodness does not hold.
[Teacher] Having heard the grandfather of the world say this, the best of the twice-born, again falling into doubt, asked:
[The sages] "What is held the most to be practised among dharmas? We see the various courses of dharma as if contradictory.
Some say there is something beyond the body, others say it does not exist; some say all is doubtful, others that there is no doubt.
Some say it is impermanent, some permanent; some that it exists, others that it does not; some say it is one form, some twofold, some mixed, some one, some separate, others plural.
Brahmins, wise and seeing the meaning of reality, think so; some wear matted hair and skins, some are shaven, some unclothed.
Some prefer not to bathe, others bathe; some want food, some are devoted to fasting.
Some praise action, others calm; some say both place and time, others that this does not exist; some praise liberation, some various enjoyments.
Some want wealth, others poverty; some say a means of worship, others that it does not exist.
Others delight in non-harm, some are intent on harm; some say it is for merit and fame, others that it does not exist.
Others delight in the good state, some stand in doubt; some say sorrow, some happiness, others meditation.
Others, steadfast, say sacrifice, others giving; some praise everything, others say not everything.
Others praise austerity, others study; some say knowledge, some renunciation, those who reflect on beings, nature.
When dharma is so stirred up and runs in many ways, we are bewildered, best of the gods, and reach no certainty.
This is best, this is best: so people proceed; whoever delights in a dharma always honours it.
There our wisdom is struck and our mind multiplied; we wish this told: what is the best, good one?
And what is the further secret, you should tell: what is the relation of goodness and the knower of the field, and by what cause?"
Thus addressed by those brahmins, the blessed, righteous, wise maker of the worlds told them truly.
[Brahma] Non-harm to all beings is held the most to be done; this is the untroubled, highest step, the mark of dharma.
The aged who see with certainty call knowledge the highest good; therefore by pure knowledge one is freed from all sins.
Those in the world who are devoted to harm and who live as unbelievers, joined with greed and delusion, go to hell.
Those who tirelessly do acts joined with hope rejoice in this world, being born again and again.
But those wise ones who do acts with faith, joined with yoga free of hope, are steadfast and see rightly.
Next I shall tell how goodness and the knower of the field are joined and separated; learn it, good ones.
It is called here the relation of object and subject: the Person is always the subject, and goodness is held to be the object.
As explained in the earlier account, as a gnat in the udumbara fig, the insentient goodness does not know it is being enjoyed; but one alone knows, who enjoys and who is enjoyed.
As long as the substance and quality last, the lamp shines; when the substance and quality are spent, the light goes to disappearance.
Goodness is manifest in quality, and the Person is held unmanifest; know this, brahmins; I shall tell you more.
A dull person does not grow even by a thousand; a wise person prospers happily even with a fourth part.
So the accomplishment of dharma is to be known by its means; the wise one who knows the means attains endless happiness.
As a man setting out on a road without provisions goes with great hardship or perishes on the way,
so in actions the fruit may or may not come; the highest good of the Self is the showing of good and bad.
As one goes a long road on foot alone, suddenly, lacking sight of reality, never seen before,
but may go that same road by a quick chariot yoked with horses, such is the way of the wise.
Having climbed a high mountain, he does not look at what is on the ground; let him see the charioteer by the chariot, the insentient one toiling.
As long as the chariot road lasts he goes by chariot; when the chariot road ends, the wise man leaves the chariot and goes on.
So goes the wise, knowing the way of union with reality, of great understanding, to higher and higher.
As one without a boat plunges into the terrible great sea with his arms alone, through delusion he surely meets death.
But as a wise man, skilled in division, enters the water by a boat with a rudder, untired, he quickly crosses, certainly.
Having crossed, he goes to the far shore, giving up the boat, free of possessiveness; as explained earlier, like the chariot-rider and the walker.
Like a boatman bewildered by affection, overcome by possessiveness, he turns round and round there.
One cannot climb a boat and turn about on land, nor ride a chariot and journey in water.
So action's varied results, each stationed in its object, come to pass as action is done in the world.
What has no smell, no taste, no form, touch or sound, what the sages think by understanding, they call Pradhana.
There Pradhana is unmanifest; the quality of the unmanifest is the great; the quality of the great, which has become Pradhana, is ego.
The quality made by the great elements belongs to ego as chief; the objects of the elements are held to be qualities separately.
As the unmanifest has the nature of seed and is of the nature of production, so we have heard the great Self has the nature of seed and production.
Ego has the nature of seed and produces again and again; the five great elements have the nature of seed and production.
They say the specifics of the five elements have the nature of seed and do not produce; know their distinction.
There space has one quality, wind is called two-quality, light three-quality, and water four-quality.
Earth is to be known as five-quality, filled with moving and immovable beings, the goddess who makes all beings, showing good and bad.
Sound, touch, form, taste and smell as fifth: these five are to be known as the qualities of earth, best of brahmins.
Earth's quality is always smell, and smell is held to be of many kinds. I shall tell its many qualities in detail.
Pleasant and unpleasant smell, sweet, sour, pungent, diffusing, compact, oily, dry and clear: so the smell of earth is to be known as tenfold.
Sound, touch, form and taste are held the qualities of water. I shall tell of knowledge of taste; taste is held to be of many kinds.
Sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, astringent and salty: so taste, made of water, is held to be sixfold.
Sound, touch and form: light is called three-quality; form is the quality of light, and form is held of many kinds.
White, black, red, blue, yellow, reddish, short, long, thick, square, minute and round.
So twelve-fold is the form of light, always to be known by brahmins who know dharma and speak truth.
Sound and touch are to be known; wind is called two-quality; touch is the quality of wind, and touch is held of many kinds.
Hot, cold, pleasant, painful, oily, clear, hard, smooth, slippery, sticky, harsh and soft.
So twelve-fold is the quality of wind, declared by rule by brahmins, perfected ones who know dharma and see the truth.
There space has one quality, and it is held to be sound. I shall tell its many qualities in detail.
Shadja, Rishabha, Gandhara, Madhyama and Panchama, and after that Nishada and Dhaivata are to be known.
Sound is pleasant or unpleasant, compact, and has divisions; so sound born of space is to be known as many kinds.
Space is the supreme element, ego beyond it, beyond ego the higher intellect, and beyond intellect the Self.
Beyond that is the unmanifest, and beyond the unmanifest the Person, who knows the higher and lower of beings, reaching whom one attains endlessness.
The mind is always the presiding one of the great beings; intellect declares lordship; the knower of the field is said to be all.
The mind yokes the senses like a charioteer good horses; the knower of the field always yokes the senses, mind and intellect.
Mounted on the chariot joined with the great elements and restrained by intellect, the self of beings runs about everywhere.
The chariot, joined with the host of senses, with mind as charioteer, restrained always by intellect, is great and made of Brahman.
The learned one who always knows the chariot so, made of Brahman, the steadfast one, does not become bewildered in any world.
From the unmanifest to the specifics, filled with moving and immovable beings, lit by the radiance of moon and sun, adorned with planets and stars,
everywhere decked with a net of rivers and mountains, ever adorned with various waters,
the livelihood of all beings, the goal of all living things: this is the Brahman-forest, in which the knower of the field wanders always.
Prajapati created all this by austerity alone, the lord; so sages gained the Vedas by austerity.
By austerity, in order, those who live on fruit and roots, perfected by austerity, composed, see the three worlds here.
Medicines, antidotes and many sciences everywhere are accomplished by austerity alone; austerity is the root means.
What is hard to get, hard to learn, hard to assail, hard to follow, all that is accomplished by austerity; austerity is indeed hard to overcome.
A drinker of liquor, a killer of a brahmin, a thief, a killer of an embryo, one who defiles his teacher's bed are freed from sin by well-practised austerity alone.
Men, ancestors, gods, animals, deer, birds and other beings, moving and immovable,
devoted always to austerity, are always perfected by austerity; so the greatly fortunate gods went to heaven by austerity.
Those who tirelessly do acts joined with hope, joined with ego, come to Prajapati's presence.
By pure meditative yoga, free of possessiveness and ego, the great souls reach the great, best world.
Approaching by meditative yoga, always serene in mind, they enter the unmanifest, an increase of happiness, by self-possession.
Approaching by meditative yoga, free of possessiveness and ego, they enter here the unmanifest, the great, best world.
Born from the unmanifest alone, the knower of the agreement has gone again, freed of darkness and passion, resting on goodness alone.
Freed from all sins, he gives up everything, without parts; know him as the knower of the field; he who knows him is a knower of the Veda.
Mind approaching mind, the sage should sit restrained; whatever his mind is, becoming that, this is the eternal secret.
From the unmanifest to the specifics is held the mark of ignorance; learn how it is thus marked by the qualities.
Death is the two-syllable word and eternal Brahman the three-syllable: "mine" is death, and "not mine" is eternal.
Some men of duller mind praise action; but the awakened great souls do not praise action.
By action the creature is born embodied, sixteen-fold; ignorance creates the Person, ungraspable, immortal-eating.
Therefore those who are free of affection for acts, who see the far shore: this Person is made of knowledge, not held to be made of action.
Unprecedented, immortal, eternal, he who finds this one beyond reasoning, who finds the ungraspable, immortal-eating Self, becomes ungraspable and immortal, firm, by these causes.
Having cast off all resolves and restrained the Self in the Self, he knows that auspicious Brahman beyond which there is nothing more.
By serenity of goodness alone one would gain serenity; the mark of serenity is like seeing a dream.
This is the goal of the liberated, who are established in knowledge; they see all activities as born of transformation.
This is the goal of the unattached, this the eternal dharma, this the gain of the knowing, this the blameless conduct.
By one equal to all beings, free of longing and hope, seeing the same everywhere, this goal can be reached.
All this has been told to you by me, best of brahmin sages; act so quickly, and then you will gain perfection.
[Teacher] So addressed by Brahma, the teacher, those sages, great souls, did so and then gained the worlds.
You too, greatly fortunate one, rightly practise what Brahma said, pure in conduct, and you will gain perfection.
[Vasudeva] So addressed by the teacher, the pupil then did the supreme dharma, son of Kunti, and then attained liberation.
That pupil, having done what was to be done, delight of the Kuru line, then reached that state going to which one does not grieve.
[Arjuna] "Who, Krishna, was that brahmin, and who the pupil, Janardana? If I may hear it, tell me that, lord."
[Vasudeva] "I am the teacher, mighty-armed one, and know my mind to be the pupil. Out of love for you this secret was told to me, Dhananjaya.
If you have love for me always, delight of the Kuru line, having heard this spiritual teaching, rightly practise it, of good vows.
Then, delight of the Kurus, this dharma being rightly practised, with self purified of all sins, you will attain liberation alone.
This very thing was said to you before by me, mighty-armed, when the time of battle was at hand; therefore set your mind on it.
I have not seen my father for a long time, lord; I wish to see him, with your leave, Phalguna."
[Vaishampayana] To Krishna who had spoken thus, Dhananjaya replied: "Let us go to the city of Gajasahvaya today, Krishna,
and meeting King Yudhishthira there, the righteous, with his leave you may go to your own city, invincible one."
So too the Pandava ordered the followers: "Make ready; we shall go to the city of Gajasahvaya."
Thus told, the soldiers made ready, O lord of the people, and reported to the immeasurably radiant Partha that all was ready.
Then Krishna and the Pandava mounted a chariot and set off, telling varied tales, pleased, O lord of the people.
To Vasudeva standing on the chariot, the greatly radiant Dhananjaya spoke again these words, best of the Bharatas.

By your grace victory was won for the king, upholder of the Vrishni line; enemies have been slain, and the kingdom without thorn gained.
mahabharata:14:51.7	The Pandavas have you as protector, Madhusudana; having reached you as a raft, we have crossed the ocean of the Kurus.
mahabharata:14:51.8	Salutations to you, maker of the universe, Self of the universe, source of the universe; as I know you and as my mind is on you,
mahabharata:14:51.9	your radiance is the source, always fire; your delight is playful, Madhusudana; sky and earth are your illusion, lord.
mahabharata:14:51.14	Even over a very long time I could not tell your virtues and the highest Self; salutations to you, lotus-eyed.
mahabharata:14:51.15	You are known to me, invincible one, from Narada and Devala, from Krishna Dvaipayana, and from the grandsire of the Kurus.
mahabharata:14:51.16	Everything rests on you, you alone are the lord of men; and what you have said, blameless one, is full of grace.
Guard all the senses like horses; they will be for good, as wealth that is protected.
Having said this to me, Hrishikesha, of inconceivable valour, left me with the children and went off to some direction, the lord.
All this has been told to you in detail, greatly radiant one: the whole story of the Kurus and the Pandavas, O Bharata.
